research.title: Memory Tax: Dissecting the Net Value of Agent Memory
research.why: Highest total in the research file (18) and the most useful finding for a general reader: in a large evaluation, many purpose-built AI-agent memory systems do worse than simply searching the raw conversation history (naive RAG). The paper splits a memory system's net value into a benefit and a 'tax', which is easy to explain. Primary source re-checked through the arXiv API. Date note: submitted to arXiv 2026-10-25, before the window, but listed on Hugging Face Daily Papers on 2026-10-28, inside it (157 upvotes). Not covered in the last 8 weeks; the closest past item, 'From Evidence to Action: How Tool-Using Agents Fail' (2026-10-10), is about tool use, not memory.
runnersUp: What Effort Level Should I Choose? Economics of Reasoning Effort in LLM Agents (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34491). Novel and easy to relate to (extra AI 'thinking' is a credence good: buyers cannot check whether it was needed), but it has little traction (32 upvotes).

Multiscale Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35013). Strong momentum (382 upvotes), but it is a technical RL credit-assignment method and hard to make accessible.

Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29927). A solid framing of how benchmarks mislead, but arXiv date 2026-10-21 is well before the window and the evaluation theme is close to recent issues.

ChronoReplay (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34283) and The Trinity (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36077). Top HF upvotes, but the abstracts were not fetched or the significance for a general reader is lower.

news.title: OpenAI, Google and Microsoft back a new standard that lets websites opt out of AI training
news.why: Kept from the prior pass. Of the news candidates, this matters most to a general reader: any website owner or creator gets a way to say no to AI training. Several primary sources agree (OpenAI post; Google Search Central https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2026/10/ai-training-control; IETF draft https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-kelley-aipref-training-preference-signal/). It is an industry technical standard, not a political or legal fight. It is not a repeat of 2026-10-24 (OpenAI no longer training on the live internet), which was about one lab's own training setup. Tell it as a mechanism story: what the signal is, who honors it, and what it does not cover.
runnersUp: Google Project Suncatcher satellite AI server sends its first response (https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-research/project-suncatcher-satellite-response/). Novel, with a strong primary source, but a demo milestone matters less to readers than a rule that affects every website.
Anthropic VS Code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours (Ars Technica). Original reporting, but no vendor advisory, so the primary source is weak.
Thrive Holdings acquires ADT for $15.3B. Has a primary source, but it is a finance deal with only a loose link to AI.

invention.title: Qwenputer: a working, deterministic RISC-V CPU running inside a Qwen3.5 language model
invention.why: Kept from the prior pass. The strongest candidate in any section (score 19; HN 695 points and 145 comments; also on Lobsters), with the builder's own write-up as the primary source. It turns the model's Gated DeltaNet state into exact RAM, which gives a concrete, surprising way to explain what is happening inside a model. Not covered before.
runnersUp: nesformer: a working NES emulator in about 1GB of Qwen weights (https://github.com/dbreunig/nesformer). Same idea with less depth. Worth a one-line 'others are doing this too' mention.
doomformer: DOOM game logic as a transformer (https://github.com/mottopanikeiku/doomformer). Same idea again.

thread: This issue is about what an AI keeps: which web pages it is allowed to learn from, whether an add-on memory system actually beats keeping the raw history, and how a model's own internal state can be turned into exact computer memory.
